criteria.name: Q1 Quality attributes
criteria.reasoning: Performance and availability are well justified from the scenario and the performance scenario is fully six-part and measurable. However, the availability response measure ('stay up most of the time') is not measurable, so not Excellent.

evidence.quote: Response measure: the system should stay up most of the time.

criteria.name: Q2 Architectural style
criteria.reasoning: Clear recommendation (modular monolith) with two trade-offs tied to scenario specifics (five developers, single VM, 20-minute deployment downtime), and the downside is explicitly acknowledged.

evidence.quote: With five developers, running eight or ten services would mean more time spent on infrastructure than on features.
The trade-off I accept is that modules cannot be scaled independently

criteria.name: Q3 Availability calculation
criteria.reasoning: Method correct throughout; series product 0.99301 and part (c) (0.999975, 0.018 h) are right. But 0.00699 × 720 = 5.0 hours, not 3.5 — one arithmetic slip, so Proficient.

criteria.name: Q4 Resilience pattern
criteria.reasoning: Circuit breaker is an appropriate pattern and application to the outage is good, but the state machine is reversed: Closed = normal flow, Open = fail fast. The core explanation is incorrect, so Developing despite tuning discussion.

evidence.quote: In the Open state calls pass through normally. When failures exceed a threshold... the breaker moves to Closed and calls fail immediately

criteria.name: Q5 Consistency and availability
criteria.reasoning: Both choices are reasonable and a concrete technique (Redis cache with TTL) is named for menu browsing, but CAP is misused (P cannot be sacrificed; partitions are a fact) and no concrete technique is named for the payment case.

evidence.quote: so for payments we choose consistency and availability and give up partition tolerance.

criteria.name: Q6 Architecture decision record
criteria.reasoning: Context, Decision and Consequences are all present and specific to the scenario, but consequences are entirely positive — no negative consequence (e.g. eventual notification delay, added infrastructure) is given.

evidence.quote: Consequences: Placing an order no longer waits for the outlet, so the response time improves.

criteria.name: Communication and format
criteria.reasoning: Questions 2 and 4 clearly exceed 150 words. Reference [2] is cited in Question 4 but missing from the reference list, which contains only one entry. Writing itself is clear and headings are correct.

evidence.quote: A rewrite would freeze feature work for months without directly fixing either problem.
[1] L. Bass, P. Clements, and R. Kazman

technical_issues.issue: Circuit breaker states reversed: Open should fail fast, Closed passes calls normally.
CAP theorem misapplied — partition tolerance cannot be given up; also no concrete technique named for the payment path.
Citation [2] (cited in Q4) is missing from the reference list.

overall: Strong scenario-specific reasoning in Q1, Q2 and Q6, but Q3 has an arithmetic slip, Q4 reverses the circuit breaker states, Q5 misuses CAP, and word limits and referencing are not fully respected.

feedback.summary: You showed strong scenario-specific reasoning in Q2 (excellent trade-offs) and good structure in Q1, Q3 and Q6. To lift your mark, fix the arithmetic slip in Q3(b), correct the reversed circuit breaker states in Q4, apply CAP correctly and name a payment-path technique in Q5, add a negative consequence to your ADR, and tighten word limits and referencing.
next_steps: Redo Q3(b): 0.00699 × 720 = 5.0 hours, not 3.5; double-check all arithmetic before submitting.
Rewrite your Q4 circuit breaker explanation: Closed passes calls normally; Open fails fast; Half-Open probes recovery.
In Q5, explain that partition tolerance cannot be sacrificed, and name a concrete technique (e.g. synchronous replication or a transactional ledger) for the payment path.
Add at least one negative consequence to your Q6 ADR and make the Q1 availability response measure measurable (e.g. '99.5% uptime per month').
Trim Q2 and Q4 to 150 words each and add the missing reference [2] to your reference list.

criteria.C1: Good choice of performance and availability with scenario-based justification, and a fully six-part, measurable performance scenario. To reach Excellent, make the availability response measure measurable — 'stay up most of the time' is not; try a percentage uptime or downtime figure per month.
criteria.C2: Excellent work: a clear modular monolith recommendation with two trade-offs tied to the scenario (five developers, single VM, 20-minute deployment downtime) and the downside explicitly acknowledged. Keep this standard.
criteria.C3: Your method was correct throughout and parts (a) and (c) were right, but one arithmetic slip in (b) — 0.00699 × 720 is 5.0 hours, not 3.5 — kept you at Proficient. Show working and recheck calculations to reach Excellent.
criteria.C4: The circuit breaker was an appropriate choice and well applied to the outage, but the state machine was reversed: Closed passes calls normally and Open fails fast. Correcting this core explanation, while keeping your tuning discussion, would reach Excellent.
criteria.C5: Both consistency/availability choices were reasonable and you named Redis with TTL for menu browsing, but CAP was misapplied — partition tolerance cannot be given up; partitions are a fact you must respond to. Also name a concrete technique for the payment path.
criteria.C6: Context, Decision and Consequences were all present and scenario-specific, but your consequences were entirely positive. Adding a genuine negative consequence (e.g. delayed order confirmation or added message infrastructure) would reach Excellent.
criteria.C7: Your writing is clear and headings are correct, but Q2 and Q4 exceed the 150-word limit and reference [2], cited in Q4, is missing from your reference list. Trimming answers and completing citations in IEEE style would lift this criterion.
